utopia.description: The book that named a genre: a sailor describes the strange island commonwealth of Utopia, where property is common, gold is worthless, and everything about European society is quietly turned on its head.
long_description: A traveler named Raphael Hythloday has seen a commonwealth unlike any in Europe: the island of Utopia, where property is held in common, gold is used for chamber pots, lawyers are banned, and six hours of work a day suffices for everyone. The author himself appears as a character in his own book — he listens, objects, and lets Raphael talk himself into the most subversive travelogue of the Renaissance.

Published in Latin in 1516, the book gave its name to an entire genre of imagined ideal societies. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

the-prince.description: The infamous handbook of power politics: how princes win states, keep them, and why it is safer to be feared than loved.
long_description: Written by a fired Florentine diplomat with nothing left to lose, this short book told princes what no one had dared put in writing: that politics is not a branch of morality. Whether to keep faith when it costs you, why armed prophets win and unarmed prophets fail, what fortune controls and what skill can seize — every question is answered with brutal, cheerful clarity and examples torn from the Italian wars.

Five centuries later it remains the most notorious book of political advice ever written. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

meditations.description: The private notebook of a Roman emperor: reminders to himself about how to stay calm, do his duty, and face death without fear.
long_description: The most powerful man in the world kept a journal that was never meant to be published. In camp on the Danube frontier, between plagues and wars, he wrote himself the same stern, humane reminders again and again: you could die at any moment, other people's opinions are not your business, and the only thing fully in your control is your own character.

That notebook became the central text of Stoic philosophy and a bedside book for readers from generals to prisoners. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

candide.description: A wide-eyed young man raised to believe this is the best of all possible worlds gets kicked around the entire globe testing the theory.
long_description: Candide is thrown out of the only home he knows, conscripted, flogged, shipwrecked, nearly eaten, and reunited with people he watched die — all while his tutor Pangloss insists that everything is for the best in this best of all possible worlds. The satire moves at sprint pace across three continents, demolishing optimism, war, religion, and colonial greed in a few thousand ruthless, hilarious words.

Published under a fake name in 1759 and banned almost immediately, it became the most read work of the French Enlightenment. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

flatland.description: A Square living in a two-dimensional world is visited by a Sphere from the third dimension, and nothing about his flat life survives the encounter.
long_description: In Flatland everyone is a shape: women are lines, workmen are triangles, gentlemen are polygons, and the priestly circles run everything. A Square narrates this geometry of society until the night a Sphere lifts him out of his plane and shows him a direction he has no word for — then asks the question that ruins him: if two dimensions can open into three, why should three be the end?

Published in 1884, it is at once a social satire, a mathematics lesson, and the founding classic of dimensional science fiction. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

true-history.description: The original science fiction: a voyage to the moon, war between the sun and moon empires, and life inside a whale — narrated by an author who promises that every word is a lie.
long_description: A ship sails past the Pillars of Hercules, gets thrown to the moon by a whirlwind, and lands in the middle of an interplanetary war fought by vulture-cavalry and spider-troops. The narrator opens by declaring that, unlike other historians, he will tell you honestly that nothing in his book ever happened — and then delivers the most inventive pack of lies in ancient literature.

Written in the second century AD as a parody of tall-tale travel writers, it is the earliest surviving story of space travel and alien war. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

decameron.description: Ten young Florentines flee the Black Death and pass ten days telling a hundred stories — bawdy, tragic, scandalous, and very much alive.
long_description: Florence, 1348: the plague is killing a city, so seven women and three men retreat to a country villa and agree to a game — each tells one story a day for ten days. The hundred tales that follow swing from con artists and lecherous friars to shipwrecked lovers and patient wives, told with an appetite for human weakness that no medieval book had dared before.

The collection became the model for storytellers from Chaucer onward. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

dialogues.description: Socrates in conversation: the trial, the prison cell, the drinking party, and the relentless questions that got him executed.
long_description: A barefoot old man wanders Athens asking people to define the words they use every day — piety, justice, courage, love — and proves, politely and devastatingly, that nobody can. These dialogues follow him through the market, a dinner party, his trial for corrupting the youth, and the cell where he drinks the hemlock, arguing to the last breath that the unexamined life is not worth living.

Written by his most famous student, they are the founding documents of Western philosophy. This Modern Classics edition retells the texts in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

common-sense.description: The pamphlet that talked a continent into independence: a plain-language demolition of monarchy and the case for an American republic.
long_description: In January 1776 most American colonists still hoped for reconciliation with Britain. Then a recently arrived English corset-maker published a shilling pamphlet arguing that kings are absurd, that an island should not rule a continent, and that the time to separate was now. Within months it had sold through the colonies at a rate no book in American history has matched since.

It remains the most effective piece of political persuasion ever printed in English. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

federalist.description: The eighty-five newspaper essays that sold a skeptical public on the United States Constitution — and still explain how it is supposed to work.
long_description: When the Constitution left Philadelphia in 1787, ratification was anything but certain. Under the shared pen name Publius, three founders wrote a barrage of newspaper essays for New York readers: why union beats confederation, why faction can be tamed but never cured, why the presidency is not a king, and why judges must guard the Constitution against the legislature itself.

The essays remain the single most cited commentary on the American constitutional design. This Modern Classics edition retells all eighty-five papers in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

democracy.description: A young French aristocrat tours Jacksonian America and writes the sharpest account of democracy — its energy, its conformity, and its future — ever produced by a visitor.
long_description: Officially he came to study American prisons. What the twenty-five-year-old French magistrate actually studied was everything else: town meetings, juries, newspapers, religion, the tyranny of majority opinion, and the restless equality that he believed was coming for Europe next, whether Europe wanted it or not.

This first volume of 1835 examines America's political machinery — and predicts, among much else, the rise of America and Russia as rival world powers. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

democracy2.description: The second volume of the great French study of America: how equality reshapes not just politics but thought, feeling, art, ambition — and how democracies can drift into a soft new despotism.
long_description: Five years after anatomizing America's political institutions, the author returned with a deeper question: what does equality do to the inside of people? This second volume of 1840 traces democracy's fingerprints on philosophy, religion, poetry, wages, families, and manners — and closes with the most famous warning in political literature, about a mild, providential despotism that reduces citizens to a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.
This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

social-contract.description: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains" — the book that asked what could make political authority legitimate, and helped ignite a revolution.
long_description: If no man has natural authority over another, why should anyone obey a government? The answer proposed here — that legitimate power can rest only on an agreement among the people themselves, expressing a general will that no king can represent — was explosive enough that the book was banned and burned within weeks of publication in 1762.

A generation later its language was in the mouths of French revolutionaries, and it has stayed in the bloodstream of democratic argument ever since. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

leviathan.description: Written in the shadow of civil war: why life without government is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short — and why we trade liberty for a sovereign to escape it.
long_description: England had just executed its king when this book appeared, arguing from first principles — matter, motion, appetite, fear — that human beings in their natural state are at war with everyone, and that the only exit is a covenant erecting an artificial man, a mortal god, the great Leviathan of the commonwealth, whose sword makes promises mean something.

It is the founding masterpiece of modern political philosophy, equal parts geometry, psychology, and menace. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

two-treatises.description: The philosophical foundation of liberal government: natural rights, property earned by labor, rule by consent, and the people's right to dissolve a government that betrays its trust.
long_description: The first treatise demolishes the fashionable theory that kings inherit their authority from Adam. The second builds something to replace it: men are born free and equal, property arises when labor is mixed with nature, government exists only by consent to protect life, liberty, and estate — and when it turns tyrant, rebellion is not a crime but a right.

Published anonymously in 1689, its sentences resurfaced almost verbatim in the American Declaration of Independence. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

wealth-of-nations.description: The book that invented economics: the division of labor, the invisible hand, and a sweeping case that nations grow rich through freedom of trade, not hoards of gold.
long_description: It opens in a pin factory, where ten workers dividing eighteen operations make thousands of pins a day that alone they could barely make at all — and from that observation builds the whole machinery of markets: prices, wages, stock, banks, rent, and the famous invisible hand by which men pursuing their own gain promote an end which was no part of their intention.

Published in 1776, it dismantled the mercantile system and founded political economy as a science. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

malthus.description: The most alarming arithmetic ever published: population grows geometrically, food arithmetically, and the gap is settled by misery — an argument that has haunted optimists since 1798.
long_description: Against the perfectibilian dreams of Godwin and Condorcet, a quiet English curate set two ratios: people multiply like compound interest, but harvests grow by addition. From that simple mismatch he derived checks that operate everywhere and always — famine, disease, war, and vice — and concluded that no utopia can outrun the pressure of population against food.

The essay reshaped economics, inspired the theory of natural selection, and made its author's name an adjective. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

progress-and-poverty.description: Why does poverty deepen as wealth explodes? A self-taught San Francisco printer's answer — land rent — became the best-selling economics book of the nineteenth century.
long_description: The puzzle is stated on the first page: everywhere the machinery of production improves, and everywhere want keeps pace with progress. The answer found here is that the gains of every advance are swallowed by the rising rent of land — and the remedy, a single tax on land values, lit a worldwide political movement that counted Tolstoy, Churchill, and Einstein among its admirers.
This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

origin-of-species.description: One long argument that changed biology forever: variation, inheritance, and the struggle for existence add up to natural selection — and to the common descent of all living things.
long_description: Twenty years of pigeon-fancying, barnacle dissection, and worldwide correspondence went into this one long argument, published in 1859 only when a letter from the Malay Archipelago threatened to scoop it. Domestic breeds, island finches, fossil strata, and the geometry of exponential increase converge on a single idea — descent with modification through natural selection — defended against every objection its author could imagine being raised.
This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

descartes.description: "I think, therefore I am": the philosophical works that doubted everything — the senses, the world, even mathematics — to find the one certainty that could rebuild knowledge.
long_description: A soldier-mathematician shut himself in a stove-heated room and resolved to demolish every opinion he had ever accepted, to see what would survive. What survived was the thinking self — and from that famous foothold he rebuilt God, the world, and a method for reasoning that promised anyone with patience could reach the truth.

These works launched modern philosophy and the analytic geometry that still bears his name. This Modern Classics edition retells the texts in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

gallic-war.description: A general's own account of conquering Gaul: eight years of campaigns, written in the third person by the man who fought them — part war report, part campaign ad.
long_description: Gaul is divided into three parts, and over eight ruthless years its conqueror took them all — bridging the Rhine in ten days to terrify the Germans, crossing to Britain twice for the spectacle of it, and finally starving the great rebellion of Vercingetorix out of the hilltop fortress of Alesia. He wrote it all up himself, in cool third-person dispatches sent home to a Rome he was preparing to master next.

It is the only great war memoir written by an author of the ancient world about his own campaigns. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

herodotus.description: The first history book ever written: the Persian Wars, plus every marvel, custom, and gossip-worthy story its insatiably curious author picked up along the way.
long_description: The project was unprecedented: find out why Greeks and Persians fought, and write it down so that great deeds would not fade with time. The result wanders gloriously — Egyptian mummification, Scythian burial mounds, gold-digging ants, the wives of Babylon — before narrowing to the story's tightest pass: a king who whipped the sea, three hundred Spartans, and the battles that saved Greece.

He has been called the Father of History and the Father of Lies; both titles are earned. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

peloponnesian-war.description: The war that broke Greece, told by a general who fought in it: plague, massacre, the Melian dialogue, and the doomed expedition to Sicily — history written as a possession for all time.
long_description: An Athenian general, exiled for arriving one day too late to save a city, spent the rest of his life writing the war between Athens and Sparta with a coldness no historian has matched since: the plague that killed Pericles, the revolutions that redefined words themselves, the envoys who told a small island that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

He promised a possession for all time rather than a prize essay for the moment, and delivered. This Modern Classics edition retells the complete text in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

montaigne.description: The invention of the essay: a retired French magistrate turns his pen on himself — on friendship, fear, cannibals, thumbs, and death — and finds the whole human condition there.
long_description: At thirty-eight he retired to his tower library, had his favorite maxims painted on the beams, and began to write about the only subject he claimed to know: himself. What do I know? became his motto, and the trials — essais — he made of his own judgment ranged over everything from the education of children to the custom of wearing clothes, always circling back to the art of living and dying well.

He invented a literary form and remains its most companionable practitioner. This Modern Classics edition retells selected essays in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

enchiridion.description: The Stoic pocket manual: fifty-one short drills for keeping your head — sort what is up to you from what isn't, and want what actually happens.
long_description: Its author was born enslaved in the Roman Empire, walked with a lame leg, and taught that no one could ever really harm him — because the only things that matter, our judgments and choices, are the only things fully in our power. His student Arrian condensed the lectures into this little handbook of drills: the broken cup, the voyage and the captain’s call, the actor handed a role, the two handles. It was a bedside book for Marcus Aurelius and for the American founders alike.

way-to-wealth.description: Twenty-five years of Poor Richard's proverbs stitched into one speech about work, thrift, and debt — delivered to a crowd that applauds every word and then ignores it.
long_description: For a quarter century, Poor Richard's Almanack scattered its maxims across the American colonies — early to bed and early to rise, no gains without pains, the sleeping fox catches no poultry. In 1758 its author gathered the best of them into a single sly performance: an old man lectures a crowd waiting for an auction on why they can't afford the very things they're about to buy. It became the most reprinted piece of American writing of its century, the founding text of the self-improvement shelf, and — thanks to its wry frame — a joke at the sermon's own expense.

memorabilia.description: Socrates remembered by his other student: not the ironist of Plato's dialogues but the practical teacher — on friendship, work, self-control, and how to be useful to your city.
long_description: Plato was not the only student taking notes. The soldier-historian who also studied with Socrates remembered a different man: less irony, more usefulness — a teacher who told a shy man to enter politics and an overconfident twenty-year-old to stay out, reconciled quarreling brothers, advised a courtesan on friendship, and answered the death-penalty charges against him with his whole way of life. It contains the Choice of Heracles — the fable of Virtue and Vice at the crossroads that John Adams wanted on the Great Seal of the United States.

de-officiis.description: Cicero's last book, written as a letter to his son: what the right requires, what advantage tempts, and why nothing dishonorable is ever truly useful.
long_description: Months after Caesar's assassination — and months before his own — Rome's greatest orator wrote his son a book-length letter on how to act. Book by book it builds a working ethics: what the four virtues demand, how to win real advantage without shame, and, in the famous finale, why every apparent conflict between the right and the useful is an illusion, argued through cases that still bite — the grain merchant at Rhodes, the ring of invisibility, Regulus keeping his promise to his executioners. It became the founders' standard manual of public ethics, and this edition is translated directly from the original Latin.

autobiography.description: The original American life story: a runaway apprentice becomes printer, scientist, and statesman — told with the dry wit of a man who brags and then winks at the brag.
long_description: A chandler's tenth son slips out of Boston at seventeen with three puffy rolls under his arms, and proceeds to invent the American success story: print shop, newspaper, almanac, library, fire company, stove, lightning rod, and a famous scheme for achieving moral perfection in thirteen weekly steps (he settles, cheerfully, for a speckled ax). Written as a letter to his son and left unfinished at the eve of the Revolution, it is the founding document of the self-made life — and funnier than its reputation suggests.

tusculan.description: Five days of dialogues at a country villa on the things that scare us most — death, pain, grief, and the passions — ending with the case that virtue alone is enough for happiness.
long_description: In the worst year of his life — his daughter dead, his republic in one man's hands — Rome's greatest orator retreated to his villa at Tusculum and spent five days arguing himself back to his feet. One day per fear: that death is no evil, that pain can be endured, that grief is not obligatory, that the soul's disorders have cures, and that virtue by itself is enough for a happy life. It contains the Sword of Damocles, and the author's own proud account of finding Archimedes' forgotten tomb. Translated directly from the original Latin.

ethics.description: The original inquiry into the good life: happiness as the goal, virtue as trained habit aiming at the mean, two books on friendship, and the case for the thinking life.
long_description: What is the good life? These lecture notes — compiled for the philosopher's son — answer with the most influential ethics ever written: happiness is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue; virtue is a habit, built by practice, aiming at the mean between too much and too little; no one becomes good by accident. Along the way: why one swallow does not make a spring, why anyone can get angry but getting angry well is rare, what friends are for, and why the life of the mind is the happiest one available to us.

roman-lives.description: The fall of the Roman Republic in five lives — Caesar, Cato, Cicero, Brutus, and Antony — by the ancient world's greatest biographer.
long_description: The ancient world's greatest biographer believed a jest or a small incident reveals more character than a battle, and these five lives prove it: the young hostage joking with pirates about crucifying them (he wasn't joking), the stubbornest man in Rome choosing death over Caesar's pardon, the orator who could not stop making enemies with his wit, the honorable assassin, and the general who threw away the world for Cleopatra. Together they tell the fall of the Roman Republic — the story the American founders read as a warning — five times over, from five angles.

seneca.description: All 124 letters from a Stoic: an old philosopher writes his friend a daily course in living — time, friendship, fear, fortune, and how to die well.
long_description: Nero's ex-minister spent his forced retirement writing letters to a friend in Sicily, and accidentally invented a genre: philosophy as daily correspondence. Each letter starts somewhere real — a noisy apartment over a bathhouse, a bout of illness, a visit to a crumbling villa — and lands somewhere permanent: guard your time, choose your company, practice poverty before it practices on you, and treat the enslaved as what they are, men. Complete in all 124 letters, ending, as its author did, unafraid.

catos-letters.description: Eighteen selected letters on liberty, power, and free speech — the anonymous newspaper columns that taught the American colonies how to argue for revolution.
long_description: After the South Sea Bubble ruined half of England, two anonymous writers signing themselves "Cato" began publishing weekly letters so incendiary that the government tried to prosecute the printer. Their doctrine — free speech is the bulwark of every other liberty, power always encroaches and must always be watched, government exists only by consent and only for the governed — crossed the Atlantic and became the common sense of the American Revolution; a sixteen-year-old Benjamin Franklin was reprinting them in Boston within a year. This selection gathers the eighteen letters the founders' generation quoted most.

galileo.description: Four days of brilliant argument about whether the Earth moves — the vernacular bestseller that got its author hauled before the Inquisition, translated from Galileo's own Italian.
long_description: In 1632 the most famous scientist in Europe published a book in Italian — not scholars' Latin — so that anyone could follow three friends in a Venetian palazzo arguing for four days about the structure of the universe: the sharp Salviati, the witty host Sagredo, and Simplicio, the earnest defender of the old order. It sold out, the Inquisition banned it, and its author spent the rest of his life under house arrest. It contains the famous ship's-cabin argument that no experiment below decks can tell you whether the ship is moving — the birth of the principle of relativity. Translated directly from the Italian.

theophrastus.description: Thirty short comic sketches of annoying people — the flatterer, the bore, the cheapskate, the newsmonger — proving human nature hasn't changed in 2,300 years.
long_description: Aristotle's successor at the Lyceum took a break from botany to write thirty ruthless little portraits of the people of Athens: the man who talks through the play, the man who remembers exactly what you owe him, the man who promises everyone everything, the man whose superstitions run his whole day. Each sketch is a definition followed by an avalanche of specific behaviors — and every single one of these people is still alive and probably in your contacts. The ancestor of all comic character writing.

twenty-thousand-leagues.description: A ten-month voyage under every sea aboard Captain Nemo's submarine Nautilus — the founding adventure of science fiction, translated complete and fresh from Verne's French.
long_description: In 1866 a mysterious sea 'monster' is terrorizing the world's shipping. Professor Aronnax joins the hunt — and, with his devoted servant Conseil and the harpooner Ned Land, is captured by the monster itself: the Nautilus, an electric submarine commanded by the brilliant, wounded, vengeful Captain Nemo. What follows is a twenty-thousand-league voyage under every ocean, half wonder and half captivity: the coral cemetery, the pearl fisheries of Ceylon, the ruins of Atlantis, the South Pole, a battle with a giant devilfish, and the maelstrom that ends it all.

For a century English readers knew this book only through the 1873 translation that cut nearly a fifth of the text, garbled Verne's science, and softened Nemo's anti-imperial fury. eighty-days.description: Phileas Fogg's £20,000 wager to circle the globe in eighty days — Verne's most delightful comic adventure, translated complete and fresh from the French.
long_description: London, 1872. The imperturbable Phileas Fogg wagers half his fortune that he can travel around the world in eighty days, and sets off that very night with his warm-hearted French valet, Passepartout. A Scotland Yard detective, certain Fogg is a fleeing bank robber, dogs him across three continents; a young widow rescued from a funeral pyre in India joins the party; and every missed steamer, typhoon, and sabotage tightens a countdown that turns on a final, famous trick of the calendar.

This Modern Classics edition retells the complete novel in brisk, witty contemporary English, translated directly from Verne's French — the fast, funny page-turner he actually wrote, with Verne's playful chapter titles and his clockwork of dates and distances kept intact.

journey-center-earth.description: Professor Lidenbrock deciphers a coded parchment and drags his reluctant nephew down an Icelandic volcano toward the Earth's core — Verne's purest wonder-and-descent adventure, translated complete and fresh from the French.
long_description: Hamburg, 1863. The formidable, gloriously irascible mineralogist Professor Otto Lidenbrock finds a runic cryptogram hidden in an old book — a message from a sixteenth-century alchemist claiming a route to the center of the Earth through the crater of a dead Icelandic volcano. Over the terrified objections of his nephew Axel, and with the imperturbable Icelandic guide Hans, the three descend into a subterranean world of bottomless galleries, a vast inner sea, forests of giant mushrooms, battling prehistoric sea-monsters, and a lost antediluvian wilderness — before a volcanic eruption hurls them back to the surface.

This Modern Classics edition retells the complete novel in vivid, propulsive contemporary English, translated directly from Verne's French — the thrilling, funny, awe-struck page-turner he actually wrote, not the heavily altered Victorian versions that renamed his characters and rewrote whole passages. Verne's 1864 geology, his Latin and runic puzzles, and his cabinet of prehistoric creatures are all kept intact.

ovid.description: The great storybook of classical mythology — from the making of the world to the transformations of gods and mortals — retold complete in vivid modern prose, fresh from Ovid's Latin.
long_description: Ovid's Metamorphoses is the single greatest storybook of classical mythology: some two hundred and fifty tales strung, in fifteen books, from the creation of the world to the death of Julius Caesar, all turning on transformation — gods into animals, mortals into trees and stones and stars, grief and desire and punishment freezing people into new shapes. It is the source almost every later poet and painter drew on: Apollo and Daphne, Phaethon's ride, Narcissus and Echo, Pyramus and Thisbe, Daedalus and Icarus, Orpheus and Eurydice, Pygmalion, Midas, and hundreds more.

This Modern Classics edition retells the complete poem — all fifteen books — in vivid, propulsive contemporary prose, translated directly from Ovid's Latin: the spellbinding, funny, sometimes horrifying, endlessly inventive page-turner it has always been, with its cosmic grandeur, tender pathos, high horror, and sly wit all kept intact, and not a single tale abridged.

soap-bubbles.description: Why a bubble is round, why a falling jet of water breaks into beads, and how a fountain can be made to sing a tune — three Christmas lectures on surface tension, given to a hall full of children and illustrated with all sixty-nine of the original plates.
long_description: Over the New Year of 1889–90, the assistant professor of physics at the Royal College of Science in South Kensington, one of the finest experimentalists of his generation, stood in front of an audience of children at the London Institution with a bench full of apparatus and gave three lectures on the skin of a liquid. Everything follows from one idea introduced in the first ten minutes: the surface of water behaves as though it were a perfectly elastic skin, always trying to make itself as small as it can. From that alone come the shape of a hanging drop, the water that climbs a narrow tube, the beads on a spider's web, a paraffined sieve that floats, bubbles nested inside bubbles, and a jet of water so sensitive that it will reproduce the tick of a pocket watch loudly enough to fill a lecture hall.

This Modern Classics edition retells all three lectures, and the complete "Practical Hints" appendix in which he explains how to build every piece of apparatus yourself, in contemporary English — with all sixty-nine of the original engravings and photographs restored, each given a descriptive caption for the first time, and with brief modern notes where a Victorian recipe calls for a material that is obsolete or genuinely dangerous.

candle.description: Six Christmas lectures for young people at the Royal Institution, drawing the whole of chemistry out of a single burning candle — where it gets its fuel, why the flame is bright, what it consumes, what it makes, and why you yourself are a slow candle.
long_description: Over Christmas 1860 the greatest experimentalist in Europe, then sixty-nine and near the end of his working life, stood in front of a hall full of children at the Royal Institution with a bench of apparatus and a candle. Everything follows from that one flame: where the wax gets up the wick (capillary attraction), why the flame has its shape (a rising current of air), why it is bright (solid particles of carbon glowing white-hot inside it), what it takes out of the air (oxygen), what it gives back (water and carbonic acid) — and finally, in the last lecture, that the burning in a candle and the breathing in your own lungs are the same chemistry, so that the analogy between a life and a taper is not a poetic figure but a literal fact.

This Modern Classics edition retells all six lectures in contemporary English, together with the separate Lecture on Platinum that the first edition appended, and restores all thirty-eight of the original woodcuts — each given a descriptive caption for the first time. The editor's explanatory notes, which sat unreachable at the back of the 1861 book behind page-number references, are placed where they belong: beside the passages they explain. The obsolete names are kept as they were spoken, with their modern equivalents glossed once, so that the reader finishes able to read other Victorian chemistry rather than holding a silent modernization.

forces.description: Six Christmas lectures for young people on gravitation, cohesion, chemical affinity, heat, magnetism and electricity — arriving at the conclusion that they are not six powers at all but one, convertible each into the others.
long_description: Over Christmas 1859 the greatest experimentalist in Europe stood in front of a hall of children at the Royal Institution and apologised: the course had twice been postponed because he was ill, he might manage only a few words, and he would substitute demonstrations for talk. Then, having claimed as always the right to speak to the young as one of them, he began — with a sheet of paper pulled over by a rubbed stick of shellac, a pendulum, a pail of water hung from the edge of a table, and a bubble of air holding up half a hundredweight of iron.

Where the Christmas course of the following year draws the whole of chemistry out of a single candle, this one takes all the powers of matter in turn — gravitation, cohesion, chemical affinity, heat, magnetism, electricity — and drives them toward one conclusion, announced in the title of the last lecture: that these are not separate forces but one force wearing different faces, each convertible into the others. Chemical action is carried along a wire and comes out as light; a coil of copper becomes a magnet; a magnet in motion makes the spark that, as the appended address on lighthouse illumination explains, was at that moment shining out to sea from the South Foreland and being noticed on the coast of France.

This Modern Classics edition retells all six lectures and the lighthouse address in contemporary English, with all fifty-nine of the original figures and with the editor's notes placed beside the passages they explain.

fleming.description: Six Christmas lectures for young people at the Royal Institution on waves of every kind — ripples on a pond, the wake of a ship, sound and music, electric oscillations, and the waves by which Marconi had just begun to signal across the sea.
long_description: Over Christmas 1901 the Royal Institution gave its young audience a course of lectures on a single idea: that a ripple crossing a pond, the bow wave of a liner, a note sung into a tube, the colour of a geranium petal and the signal Marconi had just pushed across the Atlantic are all the same thing happening in different media. J. A. Fleming — who would shortly invent the vacuum tube, and who was then the world's foremost authority on the new wireless telegraphy — begins by dropping stones into a tank of water and ends with the aerial on the coast of Cornwall.

Fleming lectures the way a good demonstrator does: everything is a thing on a table. A row of golf balls on strings stands in for the air. A flame ducks and roars when two coins are clinked across the room, hearing a note no human ear can. A prism cut from paraffin wax bends a beam nobody can see. A soap film sings. He is also a superb reporter of the science of his own moment — the air wave from Krakatoa circling the earth seven times, the guns at Queen Victoria's funeral heard 139 miles off but not at all near the Solent, the firefly's cold light that we still cannot manufacture. All eighty-seven of the original plates are here, and the argument for the aether is left exactly as Fleming made it.

ball.description: Six Royal Institution Christmas lectures taking young people from the sun out to the nebulae — with a closing chapter that teaches you to find your own way around the constellations tonight.
long_description: Sir Robert Ball, Royal Astronomer of Ireland, gave the Royal Institution's Christmas lectures in 1881 and again in 1887, and worked them up into this book. He is the warmest of the great Christmas lecturers and the funniest: he sends you off towards the sun carrying a candle, a lead bullet, a penny, a poker and a flint, and watches each of them melt in turn; he measures a ball hanging from the ceiling using two children, two cards and a pair of scissors; he works out that an express train would need 265 years to reach the sun, and that the ancients had Vulcan row it round the north each night in a boat — his only complaint being that this was all work and no play for poor Vulcan.

Six lectures carry you from the sun to the moon, out past the inner planets to Jupiter and Saturn's rings, through the comets and the great meteor showers, and finally to the stars and the nebulae — closing on a library fifty miles long that would still be too small to describe the visible universe. Ball is scrupulous about the line between what is known and what is guessed, and everything he says is left exactly as he said it, from the volcanic origin of the lunar craters to Lowell's canals on Mars. A closing chapter teaches the constellations from the Great Bear outwards, and ends by telling you not to wait for anybody to teach you: if it is clear tonight, go out and begin. All ninety-four of the original plates are here, with Ball's own captions.

thompson.description: Six Royal Institution Christmas lectures on light — from ripples in a tank of water to the X-rays discovered thirteen months before the first lecture was given.
long_description: Silvanus P. Thompson gave these six lectures at the Royal Institution over Christmas 1896, a little more than a year after Rontgen announced the rays that bear his name — and he devoted the whole of the last one to them, quoting Rontgen's own account of the discovery from an interview published only months before. A reporter asks whether the new rays are light. "No," says Rontgen. Is it electricity? "Not in any known form." What is it? "I do not know." Nothing else in this collection is this close to the event it describes.

Thompson is the reformer among the great Christmas lecturers. He believed optics was taught wrongly, and he throws out rays and angles of incidence on the first page in favour of waves in a tank of water, saying plainly that the orthodox method is fundamentally wrong. He believed that hard words, not hard ideas, are what make science look difficult — and says so in the middle of the third lecture, in a sentence that could serve as this whole series' motto: scientific men "often fall into the habit of using long and difficult words to express very simple and easy ideas."

So light is taught here as something you can watch: ripples spreading in a tank, shadows with fringed edges, a lens of air that magnifies when you drop it into oil, a Japanese bronze mirror that throws the pattern from its back onto the wall, a swan that turns black when you rotate a crystal. Then he goes past the ends of the spectrum in both directions — the ultra-violet that fogs a plate in the dark, the infra-red that lights a cigar at the focus of a mirror, Hertz's waves ten feet long, and finally the light that shows you the bones of your own hand.

All 127 surviving plates are here, recovered from the page scans of the 1897 edition, and every figure carries a descriptive caption written for this edition. The aether is left standing as Thompson's own claim, unhedged, and so is his guess about what X-rays might be.

tyndall.description: The lectures on sound that founded a tradition — from the row of boys who pass a push down a line to the fog-signal researches that overturned everything the age believed about sound at sea.
long_description: John Tyndall gave these lectures at the Royal Institution in 1867, and everything the later Christmas courses in this collection do, he does here first: the demonstration on the table, the audience addressed as people who can be shown rather than told, the argument built out of things that visibly happen. Five young assistants stand in a row with their hands on each other's backs, and the push that runs down the line is a sound wave. A glass tube is rubbed until it shivers itself to pieces. A gas flame ducks and roars at the hiss of the letter S, at the shaking of a bunch of keys, at a sixpence dropped into a hand twenty yards away — and refuses to notice anything at all if the sound is aimed half an inch above the burner.

The book runs from what sound is to what music is: the siren that counts vibrations, strings and rods and bells and Chladni's sand figures, organ pipes and the human voice, the interference that lets one sound cancel another, and finally Helmholtz's answer to a question the Greeks had asked and nobody had settled — why some combinations of notes please us and others grate. Along the way Tyndall stops to say what the scientific imagination is for, and what it costs to fix a number that others will use.

Its longest chapter is its newest. In 1873 and 1874, as scientific adviser to the Trinity House, Tyndall spent months on a steamer off the South Foreland firing guns and sounding sirens into the Channel, trying to find out how far a fog signal carries. The results contradicted each other flatly until he saw why: on days of perfect optical clearness the air can be full of invisible acoustic clouds that stop sound dead, while a dense fog is usually the clearest carrier of all. Every belief the century had inherited about fog, rain and snow deadening sound turned out to be wrong, and shipwrecks had followed from it.

All 187 plates of the third edition are here, each with a descriptive caption written for this edition, and Le Conte's 1858 paper on the sensitive flame — the observation at a musical party that started the whole line of work — is reprinted in full.

bunyan.description: The journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City — the burden that falls off by itself, the Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, and the key called Promise that was in his pocket all along.
long_description: The first part of this was written in Bedford jail, where its author spent twelve years for refusing to stop preaching without a licence, and it has never been out of print since. A man reads a book, discovers that the city he lives in is going to burn, and runs out of it with his fingers in his ears so that he cannot hear his wife and children calling him back. What follows is the most famous journey in English: the bog that swallows him, the hill he climbs on his hands and knees, the fiend who straddles the road, the valley so dark he cannot tell his own thoughts from the devil’s, the fair where his friend is burned alive, and the castle whose owner is Despair — out of which he escapes because he remembers he has had a key called Promise in his pocket the whole time.

The second part, published six years later, sends his wife Christiana down the same road, and it is a deliberate answer to the first. Christian walked alone and was terrified. Christiana has a guide, four sons, a friend, a wedding or two and a great many meals; and where Christian barely survived, the weak all get across — Mr. Feeble-mind, Mr. Ready-to-halt on his crutches, Mr. Despondency and his daughter Much-afraid. It is the warmer book, and much the funnier.

The modernization exists for an unusual reason. The book is not hard. It was written by a tinker,  in deliberately plain English for people like himself, and its sentences are short. What it is, is quietly misleading: “conversation” means conduct, “want” means lack, “prevent” means go before, and a reader sails through getting them backwards with nothing to signal the error. The allegorical names — the Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, Giant Despair, Mr. Worldly-Wiseman — are left exactly as they were written, because they are the book’s gift to the language.

tangled-tale.description: Ten comic stories with a mathematical puzzle hidden in each — and then, a month later, the author's own review of the answers his readers sent in, class-listed by pseudonym and taken apart with enormous relish.
long_description: Between 1880 and 1885 an Oxford mathematics lecturer serialised these ten “Knots” in a magazine for young women: a comic story each month with a problem buried in it, in the hope, as the preface puts it, of concealing the medicine in the jam. Two knights come down a mountain arguing about their own walking speed; a tutor and his two pupils hunt lodgings round a square; an aunt drags her niece round the Metropolitan Railway betting on how many trains they will each meet; a ship’s captain has to value five sacks of money that were weighed only two at a time; and the Governor of Kgovjni invites his father’s brother-in-law, his brother’s father-in-law, his father-in-law’s brother and his brother-in-law’s father to a very small dinner party.

The other half of the book is the part almost nobody quotes, and it is the better half. A month after each story he printed his own review of the answers that had come in — sorting his correspondents into a Class List by pseudonym, praising the elegant, and dismantling the rest with tremendous and affectionate relish. Bee’s arithmetic is faulty. Old Hen merely scratched up the earth and pecked about. Crophi and Mophi assume there were really twenty-one houses on each side, and what, one wonders, would Crophi and Mophi not assume? It is the best surviving record of what it looks like to teach mathematics to people you like.

The shillings and pence are kept exactly as they were, because several of the answers work out the way they do precisely on account of there being twelve pence in a shilling; decimalising them would quietly destroy the puzzles. Every computed answer in the book has been worked through independently — which turned up two places where the surviving text, not its author, had gone wrong.

symbolic-logic.description: The author of Alice teaching formal logic to children of twelve and fourteen — as a game, played on a squared board with red and grey counters, and with three hundred diagrams to show every move.
long_description: Carroll spent years on this book and thought it the most useful thing he ever wrote. It teaches the whole of elementary formal logic — propositions, syllogisms, soriteses, fallacies — without a single hard word that is not explained on the spot, and it teaches it as a game. You draw a square, divide it into cells, and lay counters on it: a red one to say something is there, a grey one to say nothing is. Then you read the answer off the board.

He is very funny about it. Cats understand French; a lame puppy would not say thank you if you offered to lend it a skipping-rope; three ruffians plead guilty so no verdict is returned and a whole syllogism collapses; and a friend forming a club on strictly logical principles announces that some of the members are millionaires, though the club has no members at all. The address “To Learners” that opens the book is the best short account anybody has written of how to read a hard book: begin at the beginning, do not dip, do not go on until you understand, and find a genial friend to talk the difficulties over with.

The trap in this book is not that it is difficult. It is that Carroll’s vocabulary was abandoned by the logic that came after him, so a reader with modern training is more lost than one with none. His words are kept here exactly as he wrote them — Premisses, Eliminands, Retinends, Univ., the compass geography of the diagram — because in this book the words are the machine, and it does not run without them. What has been rebuilt is everything around them: the sentences unstacked, his ditto marks written out, five hundred references to page numbers that no longer exist replaced by the chapters they point at, and a caption written for every one of the three hundred and eight diagrams saying which cell holds which counter — which the original never said at all.

pillow-problems.description: Seventy-two mathematical problems that the author of Alice worked out in his head, in bed, in the dark — and the reason he gives for doing it is not what you expect.
long_description: Carroll set himself these problems lying awake at night and solved them entirely in his head, before a diagram was drawn or a word written down. Geometry, probability, a little algebra: five beggars and a sack of pennies, a bag holding one counter that is either black or white, a wine company whose salesman is quietly robbing it, and a triangular billiard table with a pocket in every corner. The questions come first, then the answers, then the full workings.

But the Introduction is why the book is worth reprinting. He explains that he does not offer mathematics as a cure for insomnia — he says plainly he has never had it, and changed the title from “sleepless nights” to “wakeful hours” because kind friends kept writing to sympathise with an illness he did not have. What he offers it as is a remedy for “the harassing thoughts that are apt to invade a wholly-unoccupied mind”. Then he drops his guard and says which thoughts he means: sceptical ones that seem for a moment to uproot the firmest faith, blasphemous ones that dart unbidden into the most reverent souls, unholy ones that torture the fancy that would fain be pure. It is the most naked page he ever printed, and it is followed, without a break, by seventy-two problems in trigonometry.

He is very funny about himself throughout. He ends the Introduction with a list of his own mistakes — “In No. 55, I put ‘tan’ for ‘sin’”; “Apparently I was under the delusion that ‘a sin B sin C’ was the same thing as ‘sin A·bc’!” — and hopes a reader will find more, since the joy of discovery, and the intellectual superiority the reader will thereby recognise in himself over the author, may repay the time the book has cost him.

The mathematics has been reset in modern notation. Carroll's Victorian factorial, a vertical bar with the number underlined, is written “3!”; his decimal point, set at mid height, is a full stop. His prose is unstacked where it needs it and left alone where it does not — the solutions especially, which are working rather than exposition, and whose compression is the whole point of a book about what a mind can hold in the dark.

euclid-rivals.description: The author of Alice in Wonderland, in his day job as an Oxford mathematics lecturer, puts every geometry textbook of the age on trial before the ghost of Euclid — and it is a farce in four acts.
long_description: Charles Dodgson lectured in mathematics at Christ Church for twenty-six years, and in 1879 he published this: a defence of Euclid's Elements as a school textbook, cast as a stage comedy. Minos, a college examiner, is marking papers at midnight when he falls asleep over them, and is visited first by the ghost of Euclid and then by the phantasm of Herr Niemand — Mr. Nobody — a German professor who appears as counsel for each of the modern manuals in turn and is demolished in each of his briefs.

The joke is that the argument is entirely serious. Thirteen textbooks are examined, one by one, on the single question that had defeated geometry for two thousand years: how do you know that two lines will ever meet? Every rival has a way round Euclid's twelfth axiom, and Carroll shows, with great courtesy and no mercy at all, that not one of them works. Niemand's evasions get funnier as his position gets worse; he takes to coughing, then to refilling his pipe, then to threatening to vanish.

Almost nobody has read it, which is a pity, because it is the best surviving demonstration of what a Victorian mathematician actually thought he was doing when he taught a child geometry — and because it is very funny. It also contains the only known instance of a hundred-and-seventy-letter Greek dish being ordered in an Egyptian restaurant in the middle of a discussion of parallel lines.

quixote.description: The first modern novel, complete and unabridged — both volumes, all 126 chapters — retold in vivid contemporary English fresh from Cervantes' Spanish.
long_description: A dry, elderly gentleman of La Mancha reads so many books of chivalry that his wits dry up with them. He puts on his great-grandfather's rusted armour, renames his broken-down nag Rocinante, invents a peerless lady out of a farm girl he once glimpsed, and rides out to right the wrongs of the world. With him, on a grey donkey, goes Sancho Panza — a farm labourer promised the governorship of an island, who talks in proverbs and is the only man alive who loves him. Between them they take on windmills, a barber's basin, a puppet theatre, a duke and duchess who make sport of them for a hundred pages, and finally a knight in white armour on a Barcelona beach.

This Modern Classics edition retells the COMPLETE novel — Part One of 1605 and Part Two of 1615, every chapter, with all the interpolated tales that abridgements cut — in vivid, propulsive contemporary English, translated directly from Cervantes' Spanish. Sancho's avalanches of proverbs are rebuilt as English proverbs, his malapropisms remade on English words, and the verse kept as verse. The funniest book ever written, and the saddest ending in fiction, at full length and at full speed.

nights.description: Shahrazad's frame story and eighteen of the great tales of the Thousand Nights and a Night — Sindbad, the City of Brass, Aladdin, Ali Baba — retold in clear modern English from Richard Burton's 1885 translation.
long_description: A king who has been betrayed once decides to marry a new wife every night and have her killed every morning, and he keeps it up until the girls of the city are gone. Then the vizier's daughter volunteers. Shahrazad goes to the king with a plan and a sister, and at the end of the first night she stops in the middle of a story. The king lets her live one more day to hear how it comes out. She does this for a thousand nights and a night.

This is that book: the frame, and eighteen of the tales it holds. A fisherman hauls up a sealed copper jar and lets out something that has promised to kill whoever frees it. A porter carries a basket into a house of three women and is told he may stay only so long as he asks no questions. A hunchback appears to choke to death at supper and is passed from hand to terrified hand across a whole city, and every person who moves the body has a story to tell. Sindbad the Seaman comes home rich from seven voyages, each of which nearly killed him. An emir rides into the desert after Solomon's sealed jars and finds a walled city with nobody alive inside it. A boy in China is sent down a hole by a man claiming to be his uncle. A woodcutter overhears two words spoken at a rock face.

Burton's 1885 translation is the fullest in English and the least readable: he wrote it in an invented antique diction, thick with "whenas" and "hight" and "anent", which was already artificial when it was new. None of that is in the Arabic. This retelling takes the costume off and leaves the book — the comedy, the horror, the enormous appetite for detail, and the frame that holds all of it up, in which a woman keeps talking because the alternative is dying at dawn.

grimm.description: All two hundred tales and ten children's legends the Brothers Grimm collected — the famous ones and the two hundred nobody prints — retold complete in clear modern English from Margaret Hunt's 1884 translation.
long_description: A girl in a red cap meets a wolf on the forest path. A miller's daughter is locked in a room full of straw and told to spin it into gold by morning. A boy who cannot shiver goes out to learn how. These are the tales everybody knows, and the Brothers Grimm collected them alongside two hundred others that almost nobody prints: a hedgehog who beats a hare in a footrace by cheating, a soldier who traps the Devil in a boot with no sole, three army surgeons who take out their own eyes and hearts overnight and get them back in the wrong bodies, a lie-tale in which two roasted chickens fly past with their breasts turned to heaven.

This edition is all of it — two hundred tales and ten children's legends, in the order the Grimms left them, retold in clear modern English. Nothing is abridged and nothing is left out, including the tales later editors quietly dropped. Margaret Hunt's 1884 version, the first complete English Grimm and still the only one in the public domain, is the text underneath; what has changed is the language. Hunt wrote for Victorians and kept the thees and thous and the inverted sentences, and behind that surface lies a subtler trap: her “conversation” means conduct, her “want” means lack, her “prevent” means go before. A reader trips on “hath” and knows to look it up; the same reader walks straight past “prevent” and comes away confidently wrong.

What is left when the Victorian varnish comes off is not the nursery. The tales are funny, brutal, matter-of-fact and very fast. Stepmothers are murdered, giants are outwitted by tailors, God and St. Peter walk the roads asking for bread, and the rhymes the animals speak in — which are the oldest part of any of it — still rhyme.

epictetus.description: The lectures the Enchiridion was cut down from: a former slave, in a provincial classroom, telling Rome's young gentlemen that they are the ones in chains.
long_description: Everyone has read the Enchiridion. Almost nobody has read the book it came out of. Epictetus was born enslaved in Phrygia, owned in Rome by a freedman of Nero's, lame in one leg, and expelled from the city with the other philosophers by Domitian; he spent the rest of his life teaching in a Greek provincial town, and he wrote nothing. What survives is his pupil Arrian's shorthand of the actual classroom — four of an original eight books — and Arrian insists in the opening letter that he did not write them and did not make them public.

So this is not a handbook of rules but a man talking out loud: answering hecklers, losing patience, breaking off to ask a student whether he came to be flattered or to be improved. It is where the famous drills come from, with the arguments left in, and it is far funnier than its reputation. A twice-consul who flatters, he says, is more a slave than a man who has been sold three times; and if you doubt it, go and ask a friend of Caesar when he last slept quietly.
This Modern Classics edition retells all four books complete in contemporary conversational English, faithful to the original meaning but meant to be genuinely fun to read.

subjects: Knowledge, Theory of -- Early works to 1800
hume.description: The book that broke causation: why no amount of experience can prove the sun will rise tomorrow, and why it does not matter.
long_description: David Hume thought his masterpiece had failed because he had written it badly. The Treatise of Human Nature, he said, “fell dead-born from the press”; so at thirty-seven he took its hardest arguments, threw out the scaffolding, and rewrote them as twelve short essays a person could read in an evening. He spent the rest of his life insisting that this, and not the Treatise, was the book to judge him by.

The arguments are still the most unsettling in philosophy. We believe the future will resemble the past — but every argument for that belief already assumes it, so the belief has no foundation in reason at all. We believe one thing causes another — but look as hard as you like at one billiard ball striking a second and you will never see the causing, only the one thing and then the other. What we call necessity turns out to be a habit of expectation in us, not a link in the world. And having demolished the whole structure, Hume shrugs: nature has not left this up to reason. “Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.”

Along the way he explains why no testimony could ever establish a miracle, in a chapter that kept him out of two universities; puts the case against providence into the mouth of a friend, so as not to have to make it himself; argues that free will and determinism were never actually in conflict; and ends by telling us to burn any book that contains neither mathematics nor evidence.

None of this is difficult prose. Hume is one of the great stylists in English and his famous sentences are already perfectly clear. What dates is the machinery around them — “matter of fact,” “relations of ideas,” “the operations of the understanding” — a technical vocabulary that looks like ordinary English and is not, so that a modern reader glides past it and comes away confidently wrong. This edition clears that away and leaves the prose alone, keeping every one of Hume's italics, which are part of the argument rather than decoration.

augustine.description: The first autobiography: a brilliant, restless man tells God everything, and invents the inner life on the way.
long_description: Nobody had written a book like this before. In about 397, the bishop of a small North African port sat down and told God the story of his own life — not a defence, not a chronicle of deeds, but an account of what it had actually been like to be himself: the stolen pears he did not even want, the friend whose death made his own country unbearable, the woman he lived with for fifteen years and dismissed, the years of putting off a decision he had already made. Out of it came the divided will, the self that is a problem to itself, the memory you walk through like a country. We have been writing about our interior lives in his terms ever since.

Every sentence is addressed to God — not about him, to him. Augustine narrates his own life to somebody who already knows all of it, which is a strange and deliberate position, and it is why the book feels the way it does. He is not explaining himself to us. We are overhearing.

And he is much faster and funnier than his reputation. He prays for chastity and self-control, "but not yet", and knows exactly how funny that is. He is jealous of a drunk beggar in a Milan street who is happier than he is. He hated Greek homework. He breaks off mid-argument to ask whether he has just said something stupid.

The last four books are not a memoir at all, and most modern editions cut them. They are kept here entire. Book Ten is why the Confessions is read in psychology departments; Book Eleven contains the greatest sustained writing about time in any language, and the most famous confession of ignorance in philosophy: "What is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know."

This edition works from E. B. Pusey's translation of 1838, the classic English Confessions and the one that made "Thou" the voice of the book in English. That measures at the highest archaism density in this whole collection — and nearly all of it is one grammatical feature. The central decision here is that Pusey's "Thou" is rendered as "you": Latin tu is the intimate singular, the pronoun you use with a friend or a child, so the Victorian "Thou" makes the book considerably more formal than Augustine wrote it. What is recovered is something Pusey's readers never had.

boethius.description: A condemned man in a prison cell is visited by Philosophy, who tells him that nothing he has lost was ever his.
long_description: In 523 Boethius was the most powerful civilian in Italy: consul, head of the government, the last Roman who could still read Greek philosophy in the original and was trying to translate all of it before it was lost. Within a year he was accused of treason, condemned without a hearing, and held in a cell at Pavia waiting to be executed. There he wrote this book, and then he was clubbed to death.

It begins as self-pity. A ruined man sits with the Muses of poetry helping him write down how badly he has been treated, and a tall woman appears in the room and throws them out — they are making the sickness worse, and she has come to cure it. What follows is a conversation between the two, alternating prose argument with thirty-nine poems, in which Philosophy dismantles everything her patient thought he had lost. Fortune never promised to stay; that is what the wheel means, and Boethius is the reason the wheel is in every medieval manuscript. Wealth, office, power, fame and pleasure are not five goods but five broken pieces of one. The wicked are not getting away with it, because getting away with it is the punishment. And in the last book, the hardest question of all: if God already knows what you will do tomorrow, in what sense do you choose it? His answer — that God does not foresee anything, because God has no future to see it in, but holds all of time at once in a present that never passes — is one of the great moves in the history of thought, and Aquinas took it over whole.

It became the most-read book in Europe after the Bible. Alfred the Great translated it into Old English, Chaucer into Middle English, Elizabeth I into her own hand. Dante built the Paradiso out of it. And there is not one Christian doctrine anywhere in it: a Christian writing under sentence of death consoled himself entirely with reason.

This edition is a modern English retelling of H. R. James's 1897 translation, with all five books and all thirty-nine poems complete — the poems kept as poems, in verse, which is how Boethius wrote them and the half of the book that abridgements cut.

mill.description: One principle: the only thing that entitles anyone to interfere with your freedom is preventing harm to somebody else.
long_description: John Stuart Mill was raised as an experiment. His father started him on Greek at three and algebra at eight, and by twenty he had read more than most scholars read in a lifetime and had suffered a breakdown he traced directly to the training. He spent the rest of his life arguing that a human being is not a machine built to a model but a tree, which has to grow on every side.

On Liberty, published in 1859, asserts one very simple principle and then spends five chapters finding out what it costs. The only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. Not his own good, physical or moral. Not that it would make him happier, or that everyone else thinks it wise, or even that it is right. Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.

What follows is the best case ever made for free speech — not that the censor might be wrong, though he might, but that a truth nobody is allowed to argue with dies inside the people who hold it, and becomes a dead dogma rather than a living truth. Then comes the argument about individuality, which is the most beautiful writing in the book, and then the hard part: the limits of what society may forbid, worked through on drink, gambling, education, marriage, and the case Mill puts hardest against himself. He was writing against a new danger and he named it: not the tyranny of a king but the tyranny of the majority, which leaves fewer ways out, penetrates deeper into the details of life, and enslaves the soul itself.

This edition is a modern English retelling, complete and unabridged, with Mill's own footnotes kept in place and his dedication to Harriet Taylor, who he said was in part the author of everything best in his writings.

subjection.description: Written in 1861, held back for eight years, published fifty years before British women could vote: the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong, and nobody has ever tried the alternative.
long_description: Mill wrote this in 1861 and then put it in a drawer. He judged that the public was not ready for it, and he was probably right; when it finally appeared in 1869 it was met with ridicule from people who had admired On Liberty ten years earlier. British women would not get the vote for another fifty years.

The argument is in four moves. First: we do not actually know what women are like, because the question has never been put to the test — what is called the nature of women is an eminently artificial thing, the result of forced repression in some directions and unnatural stimulation in others, and you cannot learn the nature of anything by studying it only in chains. Second, and hardest: what the law of marriage actually said in 1869, set out point by point against what the law of slavery said, with the conclusion that marriage is the only actual bondage known to our law, and there remain no legal slaves except the mistress of every house. Third: that no occupation should be closed to anybody by an accident of birth, since the only way to find out what a person can do is to let them try. And fourth, the question the sceptics really want answered — what would anyone actually gain?

His answer to that last one is the surprising part. Not primarily that women would gain, though they would, but that men would: that a boy who grows up believing himself the superior of half the human race by birth alone is being taught a lesson that deforms him, and that a man who chooses a companion he cannot be challenged by has arranged to stop learning. The real obstacle, Mill says flatly, is not any doubt about what women can do. It is that most men cannot yet tolerate the idea of living with an equal.

This edition is a modern English retelling, complete and unabridged, with Mill's own footnotes kept in place. It is the companion to On Liberty, whose dedication to Harriet Taylor Mill points straight at it.

burke.description: The book that invented conservatism, written in 1790 by a Whig who had spent his career attacking the abuse of power in America, Ireland and India.
long_description: Edmund Burke had spent thirty years in the House of Commons attacking the abuse of power. He defended the American colonists, argued for the Irish, and spent seven years prosecuting Warren Hastings for what the East India Company had done in Bengal. So when the Bastille fell and London clubs began congratulating the French on their revolution, Burke was expected to join in. Instead he wrote this, and lost most of his friends over it.

It takes the form of a letter to a young Frenchman who had asked his opinion, and it is not a defence of kings. Burke's argument is that a society is not a machine that can be taken apart and reassembled to a drawing, because most of what holds it together was never designed by anybody: it is habit, affection, inherited obligation, and a great deal of accumulated prejudice that turns out on inspection to contain more wisdom than the men pulling it down possess between them. Rage and frenzy, he says, will pull down more in half an hour than prudence and foresight can build up in a hundred years.

Written in 1790, while the Revolution was still in its hopeful phase, it predicted the confiscations, the collapse of the currency, the revolutionary tribunals, and at the end of it a popular general who would draw the eyes of all men upon himself and become master of the whole republic. Napoleon was twenty. That is why the book has never gone away, and why its admirers and its opponents have both been arguing with it ever since.

This edition is a modern English retelling, complete and unabridged, with all of Burke's footnotes kept in place, his long quotations of French and Latin given in English alongside the originals, and nothing softened—including the passages his own century thought extravagant and ours thinks worse.

spinoza.description: Everything that exists is one substance, which you may call God or Nature; understanding that is the only freedom there is.
long_description: Spinoza was expelled from his synagogue at twenty-three with a curse read over him, ground lenses for a living, refused a chair at Heidelberg, and left this book to be published after his death because printing it while he lived would have been dangerous. It is the most uncompromising book in European philosophy, and it is laid out like Euclid: definitions, axioms, and two hundred and fifty-nine propositions, each one proved from the ones before it.

The argument is that there is only one substance. Spinoza calls it God or Nature, and means that the two words name the same thing: not a person who made the world and watches it, but the world itself, considered as the single system whose necessity everything follows from. There are no miracles and no purposes in it. Nature has no goal in view, and the belief that it does is traced, in the Appendix to Part One, to men's being conscious of what they want and ignorant of why they want it. That Appendix is the finest prose in the book and is why many people read it at all.

From there the argument turns to us. Mind and body are not two things but one thing described two ways. Free will is an illusion of the same kind as final causes: we feel free because we know our desires and not their causes. Every emotion is treated with the flatness Spinoza promises in the Preface to Part Three, where he says he will consider human actions and desires exactly as if he were dealing with lines, planes and solids, and then does. Forty-eight emotions are defined in order, hatred and jealousy and ambition among them, with no more moralising than a geometer gives a triangle.

And the end of it is not resignation. Bondage is being pushed about by things you do not understand; freedom is understanding them, and the two are the same act. A free man thinks of death least of all things. Blessedness is not the reward of virtue but virtue itself. The last sentence of the book has been quoted ever since: all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.

This edition does one thing no earlier English edition does. The Ethics is bound together by more than a thousand cross-references, and Elwes prints them as Spinoza's contemporaries did -- “(II. vii. Coroll.)”, “(by the last Prop.)”, in a hundred and thirty-seven different shapes. Every one of them has been resolved and written out in full, so that a reader can follow a proof without counting on their fingers.
