wollstonecraft.description: Written in six weeks, three years after the Revolution: women are not born frivolous, they are made so by an education that gives them nothing else to be.
long_description: Wollstonecraft wrote this in six weeks at the beginning of 1792, three years after the fall of the Bastille, and dedicated it to Talleyrand, whose plan for French national education had just proposed that girls be taught at home until they were eight and then no further. Her dedication tells him to his face that he treated the subject far too quickly, and adds: I plead for my sex, not for myself.

The central claim is stranger and harder than the one her reputation suggests. It is not simply that women are equal to men. It is that nobody has the slightest idea what women are like, because the character women actually have is an artefact of the way they are brought up. Taught from infancy that beauty is woman's sceptre, the mind shapes itself to the body, and, roaming round its gilt cage, only seeks to adorn its prison. Take a creature, deny it any serious occupation, tell it from birth that its whole business is to please, punish it for every deviation, and then point to the result as proof of what it is by nature.

So she goes after the men who wrote the rules. A third of the book is a demolition of the conduct manuals every girl of her class was raised on: Rousseau, who wanted Sophia educated to be a delightful companion and taught a useful subtlety; Dr. Gregory, who advised his daughters to conceal any learning they had and to feign poor health; Dr. Fordyce, whose sermons she quotes at length and simply lets stand. The demand she puts in their place is not for privileges but for the thing that makes privileges unnecessary: an education in reason, work that pays, a civil existence in the state, and coeducational national schools where girls and boys learn side by side. Along the way she asks, almost in passing and fifty years before anyone else, why women have no representatives in Parliament.

She is also much funnier and much angrier than she is given credit for. She wishes to see the distinction of sex confounded in society, and says so knowing it will raise a horse laugh. She calls the divine right of husbands what it is, by analogy with the divine right of kings. And she is savage about women as they are — vain, cunning, idle — because that is the whole point: this is what the education produced.

This edition is a modern English retelling, complete and unabridged, with all thirteen chapters, the Dedication, the Introduction and all thirty-seven of Wollstonecraft's own footnotes. The chapter titles are hers, restored from the 1792 printing.

sun-tzu.description: The oldest surviving book on war, and the one that says the highest skill is to win without fighting at all.
long_description: Sun Tzu wrote about six thousand Chinese characters some time in the fifth century BC, and they have been read by soldiers ever since. The Art of War is not a manual of battle drill. It is an argument that war is ruinously expensive, that a long war has never yet done a country any good, and that the whole business is therefore to be settled by knowing more than the other side and by moving before he is ready. Its most famous sentence says that to win a hundred victories in a hundred battles is not the height of skill; the height of skill is to break the enemy's resistance without fighting.

What makes this edition worth having is what most editions leave out. For two thousand years Chinese generals and scholars wrote their commentaries into the margins, and eleven of them are printed here alongside the text: Ts'ao Kung, who was himself a warlord and the earliest annotator; Tu Mu, who was a poet; Li Ch'uan, Mei Yao-ch'en, Chang Yu and the rest. They disagree with Sun Tzu, they disagree with each other, and they illustrate him with the histories -- Han Hsin drawing up his army with a river at its back so that it could not run away, Pan Ch'ao burning a camp at midnight with thirty-six men, T'ien Tan's oxen with blazing twigs tied to their horns. More than half this book is that argument, going on down the centuries.

This retelling works from Lionel Giles's 1910 translation, the first accurate one in English, and modernises his Edwardian prose and his scholarly apparatus. Giles's own footnotes are kept, because several of them are the best thing on the page.

inferno.description: A man lost in a dark wood is taken down through Hell by a dead poet, and meets the people he knew.
long_description: Dante Alighieri was exiled from Florence in 1302 under sentence of death by burning, and never went home. Some time afterwards he began a poem in which a man of thirty-five, lost in a dark wood, is led down through the whole of Hell by the ghost of Virgil. It is the first great work of European literature written in an ordinary spoken language rather than in Latin, and it is largely responsible for the fact that Italians speak Italian.

What makes the Inferno unlike any other vision of the afterlife is that it is full of people the author knew. Popes, neighbours, bankers, a former teacher, the man who betrayed his city, two lovers he had probably met — they are all down there, named, still arguing about Florentine politics, still furious, and still perfectly certain they were in the right. Francesca explains how she and her brother-in-law came to be caught, and blames the book they were reading. Ulysses tells how he sailed past Gibraltar and drowned. Ugolino describes eight days in a locked tower with his sons and then stops, at the one line nobody has ever been able to settle.

This retelling works from the Italian and keeps the shape Dante wrote in: thirty-four cantos, four thousand seven hundred and twenty lines, tercet for tercet, in clear modern English. What it does not attempt is the rhyme. Dante's interlocking triple rhyme cannot be carried into English without padding, and padding a poem this compressed would cost more than the rhyme is worth.

cellini.description: A Florentine goldsmith tells his own story: popes, murders, a prison escape, and the casting of the Perseus.
long_description: Benvenuto Cellini began dictating his life to a thirteen-year-old boy while he went on working, and stopped in the middle of a sentence about twenty years later. In between he set jewels for two popes, fired the guns of the Castel Sant'Angelo during the sack of Rome (and claims the shots that killed the Constable of Bourbon and wounded the Prince of Orange), killed several men, went to France for Francis I, made the gold saltcellar that is now in Vienna, broke his leg escaping over the wall of a papal prison, was poisoned, and cast the bronze Perseus that still stands in the Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence.

It is the first autobiography by an artist, and it survives because it is impossible to put down. The famous night of the casting is here in full — the workshop roof on fire, the metal curdled in the furnace, Cellini in bed with a fever, getting up to throw two hundred pewter plates and bowls into the melt — and so is the salamander in the fire that his father made him remember with a box on the ear, and the vision of the sun in the prison, and the shouting match with Bandinello in front of the Duke. He is boastful, litigious, devout, funny without meaning to be, and quite certain throughout that he has been wronged.

This retelling works from Cellini's Italian rather than from a Victorian English version, and keeps the thing that makes him himself: the headlong spoken sentences of a man talking, not writing. Nothing is abridged and nothing is tidied — the violence, the two women he treated badly, and the boasting all stand as he dictated them, because a Cellini with his edges filed off is not Cellini but a story about a Renaissance craftsman.

purgatorio.description: The second book of the Comedy: a mountain in the southern sea where the dead are being changed, and where the dead are glad.
long_description: Hell is a place where nothing can happen. Purgatory is the opposite: everyone on this mountain is going to be saved, knows it, and is being altered on the way — which makes the second book of the Divine Comedy the most human of the three, and the one that readers who know only the Inferno are most surprised by. The souls here embrace, apologise, tease, ask after old friends and beg for prayers. A musician sings a love song of Dante's own and the whole crowd stops to listen until an old man shouts at them to get moving. A Florentine sits behind a rock making fun of the climb. A poet meets the poet who converted him without knowing it.

It is also the only cantica with weather and a clock. There is a sunrise on the shore, three nights when climbing is forbidden and the travellers sleep on the steps, three dreams before dawn, and a sun whose position Dante keeps checking. Seven terraces take the seven deadly sins in order, and on each one the punishment is chosen to teach rather than to hurt: the proud carry stones, the envious have their eyes sewn shut, the wrathful walk in smoke, the lustful walk in fire. At the summit there is a wood, a river that takes away the memory of sin, and a woman Dante last saw when he was twenty-five.

This retelling works from the Italian and keeps the shape Dante wrote in: thirty-three cantos, four thousand seven hundred and fifty-five lines, tercet for tercet, in clear modern English. As in the Inferno, it does not attempt the rhyme — terza rima cannot cross into English without padding, and padding is what a poem this compressed must never suffer. The Latin the mountain sings is left as Latin, because the souls are singing it.

paradiso.description: The third book of the Comedy: out through the spheres to the light, and the last words of the greatest poem in Europe.
long_description: The Paradiso has a reputation for being the difficult one, and it is the book Dante himself thought was his best. He had put the dead in Hell and changed them on the mountain of Purgatory; here he has to write about happiness, which is much harder, and about a place where there is nothing left to want. His answer is to make the whole cantica out of light — a dozen different words for it, used as carefully as a physicist uses units — and then, whenever the argument climbs, to reach for the smallest thing in the room. Heaven in this poem is a bird on the nest waiting for dawn, a baby flinging its face towards the milk, jackdaws warming their feathers, wheels turning in a clock, a tailor cutting the gown to the cloth he has.

It is also much angrier and much more personal than its reputation suggests. Saint Peter goes red in the face and calls the papacy a sewer. Dante's great-great-grandfather, a crusader killed in the Holy Land, tells him he is going to be exiled and that he will find out how salt another man's bread tastes — the most famous thing anybody says about exile in any language. Two pagans turn up among the saved, and Dante knows perfectly well how startling that is. And at the very top, after thirty-three cantos of saying that he cannot say it, he sees three circles of three colours, gives up, and finishes the poem in a single line about a wheel turning evenly.

This retelling works from the Italian and keeps the shape Dante wrote in: thirty-three cantos, four thousand seven hundred and fifty-eight lines, tercet for tercet, in clear modern English. As in the Inferno and the Purgatorio, it does not attempt the rhyme — terza rima cannot cross into English without padding, and padding is what a poem this compressed must never suffer. Dante's Latin is left as Latin, with the English folded into the same line where a reader would otherwise be locked out.

subjects: Odysseus, King of Ithaca (Mythological character) -- Poetry
odyssey.description: The oldest adventure story in Europe: ten years of monsters and shipwrecks, and then the harder half, a man getting his house back.
long_description: A man has been away from home for twenty years — ten at the war and ten trying to get back — and everybody has given him up except his wife, who is holding off a houseful of suitors eating her out of her own halls, and his son, who was a baby when he left. That is the whole plot, and it has been the model for stories about going home ever since.

It is far stranger and funnier than its reputation. A giant with one eye is blinded with a sharpened olive stake and then outwitted by a man who says his name is Nobody, so that when the other giants ask who is hurting him he shouts that nobody is. A witch turns the crew into pigs, and they keep their own minds inside the pigs' heads. Odysseus goes down to the dead and meets his own mother, who did not know he was alive, and three times tries to hold her and three times she goes through his arms. And Achilles, the greatest of the Greeks, tells him he would rather be a hired labourer for some poor farmer on earth than king over all the dead.

The second half is quieter and crueller. Odysseus comes home disguised as a beggar and is kicked, insulted and pelted in his own hall by men eating his food, and has to take it. His old dog recognises him, lying on a dung-heap, wags his tail, and dies. His nurse recognises him by a scar while washing his feet, and he catches her by the throat. And his wife, who is as careful as he is, will not believe he is her husband until she has set him a trap of her own and he has walked into it.

This retelling works from the Greek — the text of the 1919 Loeb, all twenty-four books and nothing abridged — and is set as prose, which is what an English reader of a novel-length story actually wants. The formulas are kept and kept consistent, because they are the poem's machinery and not its decoration: the rosy-fingered dawn, the wine-dark sea, Odysseus who endures everything.

dogen.description: Two short instructions from the founder of Sōtō Zen: how to sit, and how to study. From the Chinese, complete.
long_description: In 1227 a Japanese monk came home from four years in China and wrote a page and a half on how to sit down. That is the Fukanzazengi. It tells you which foot goes on which thigh, where to put your hands, that your ears should line up with your shoulders and your nose with your navel, that the tongue rests on the palate and the eyes stay open. Then, in the middle of the posture instructions and in exactly the same voice: think of the thing that does not think; how do you think of the thing that does not think; beyond thinking.

The second piece, the Gakudō Yōjinshū of 1234, is ten short sections of advice to people taking the practice up, and it is blunter than anything in his reputation. Do not look for an easy practice; a man who wants what is easy has told you already that he is no vessel for it. Do not practise for reputation, or reward, or miraculous powers. As for the teachers of his own country, he will not allow them a single one: they hand down written words and set people reciting names, and day and night they count another man's treasure and have not half a coin of their own. If you cannot find a real teacher, he says, better not to study at all.

He is not vague and not soothing, and English has made him both. He is a man giving instructions, and he is entirely certain. The argument the two pieces share is the one his whole school rests on: sitting is not a technique for getting somewhere, because there is nowhere to get to. The way is already complete. So what is practice for? These are the answer.

This retelling works from the kanbun — the classical Chinese he wrote in — using Eiheiji's own collected edition of 1909. There is no public-domain English version of either text, so unlike every other translated volume in this collection this one has no earlier version standing beside it as a check.
